questions.stem: In an ecosystem, energy flows through trophic levels while nutrients are recycled. Why does energy need a continuous input from the Sun, while carbon and nitrogen can be recycled?

options.text: Energy is destroyed at each trophic level, but nutrients are indestructible

Energy is converted to heat through respiration at each level and lost to the environment, so it cannot be recycled; matter (nutrients) is not lost - it is converted between different forms and reused
The Sun provides both energy and nutrients to ecosystems
Energy is recycled through decomposition, just like nutrients

questions.explanation: Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction. At each trophic level, organisms use energy for respiration, releasing it as heat - a form that cannot be recaptured by living organisms. This is why continuous sunlight input is needed. In contrast, atoms of carbon, nitrogen, and other elements are not used up; they are converted between organic and inorganic forms and recycled through biogeochemical cycles.

questions.stem: An ecologist wants to assess the overall health of a river ecosystem. She measures species diversity (number of different species) at several points along the river. Near a sewage outfall, she finds only 3 species in high numbers. Upstream, she finds 25 species. What does this data suggest?

options.text: The sewage outfall has improved the ecosystem by increasing population sizes
Low species diversity near the outfall indicates pollution; only pollution-tolerant species survive, while many sensitive species have been eliminated
The upstream area must also be polluted because it has too many species
Species diversity has no connection to ecosystem health

questions.explanation: Species diversity is a key indicator of ecosystem health. High diversity (25 species upstream) indicates a healthy, unpolluted environment. Low diversity near the sewage outfall (only 3 species, likely pollution-tolerant ones like bloodworms) indicates environmental stress. Sewage causes organic pollution that depletes dissolved oxygen, killing most species except those adapted to low-oxygen conditions.

questions.stem: A student needs to explain the connections between the carbon cycle, energy flow, and population dynamics. Which statement correctly links all three concepts?

options.text: Carbon, energy, and populations are independent of each other

Producers fix carbon from CO2 into glucose (carbon cycle) using light energy (energy flow); consumers obtain this carbon and energy by eating; population sizes are limited by the amount of energy and nutrients available at each trophic level
Energy drives the nitrogen cycle, which determines carbon availability, which controls populations
Populations create energy through respiration, which drives nutrient cycles

questions.explanation: These three concepts are deeply interconnected. Photosynthesis links the carbon cycle and energy flow by using light energy to fix atmospheric CO2 into organic carbon compounds. Energy transfers through food chains determine how much energy reaches each trophic level. The available energy and nutrients at each level limits the biomass and therefore the population size that can be supported.

questions.stem: Climate change is causing global temperatures to rise. How might this affect ecosystems in the UK?

options.text: All UK species will benefit from warmer temperatures
Some species may extend their range northward, while others adapted to cooler conditions may decline; seasonal timings may shift, disrupting food chains
UK ecosystems will be unaffected because the temperature change is too small
All species will migrate south to find cooler conditions

questions.explanation: Climate change has complex effects on ecosystems. Warmer conditions allow some species to expand northward (e.g., some insects and birds have already shifted ranges). However, cold-adapted species may decline as their habitat shrinks. Crucially, climate change can disrupt ecological timing - for example, if plants flower earlier but pollinators have not adjusted, food webs can be disrupted. These phenological mismatches threaten biodiversity.

questions.stem: A GCSE student is asked to design an investigation into the effect of light intensity on plant distribution across a school field, from a shaded area under trees to an open sunny area. Which combination of equipment and method would be most appropriate?

options.text: Pitfall traps placed randomly across the field
A line transect from shade to sun, with quadrats placed at regular intervals along it, and a light meter to measure light intensity at each quadrat position
Random quadrats across the whole field with a thermometer at each
Capture-recapture of plants along the field boundary

questions.explanation: A transect from shade to sun is the correct method because it measures changes along an environmental gradient (light intensity). Quadrats at regular intervals allow plant species to be identified and their abundance measured at each point. A light meter measures the abiotic factor being investigated. This systematic approach directly tests whether plant distribution correlates with light intensity. Random sampling would not show the gradient pattern.
